notes.urn:cts:latinLit:tmp1163.tmp1163.opp-lat: Line 19 (ch. 17 of the list): 'evangelica' is marked by the edition as doubtful; taken as 'evangelia', compare 'altario vel Evangelio' in the Rule itself. Line 24 (ch. 22): *laia* and *lactina* are obscure colour or cloth terms, left untranslated; *lactina* may mean milk-white, and *laia* is uncertain and may be corrupt. Line 29 (ch. 27): 'Manent' is taken as 'maneat', and the title may be incomplete; the sense may concern the abbess sleeping or staying with the community. Lines 18 and 58 (chs. 16): 'to receive an infant from baptism' means to act as its godmother. Line 47 (ch. V): 'inaequalitas' is taken in its late Latin sense of ill health; the sense is not certain. Line 57 (ch. XV): 'marcionibus' is taken as masons. Line 54 (ch. XII): the edition's sentence ends in a comma and may be incomplete. Line 60 (ch. XVIII): the syntax of the end of the sentence is awkward and the punctuation has been adjusted; 'absque abbatissa' may belong with what follows. Line 59 (ch. XVII): *posticium* is rendered 'postern' (a back gate or door).

XXII: *laia* is obscure; it is usually taken as a natural or undyed colour, and the sense is uncertain. XXXV: *allilia* is read as *altilia*, fattened fowl. XXXVIII: *dici e* is read as *dicite*. *Missae* in this rule does not mean Mass; here it denotes a unit of the office made up of readings with prayer, and is left untranslated. In the order of psalmody, psalm and canticle incipits are translated, and hymn incipits are left in Latin as titles. The sense of *capitellum* (rendered as a short closing verse) and of *directaneus* (a psalm said straight through) is inferred from liturgical usage. *Hic est dies vernus Dei* is read as *verus*, the usual title of the hymn. *Benedictio* at Easter matins is probably the canticle of the three young men (Benedicite), though the text does not say so. 'Una soror legat paginas, aut quatuor': a numeral seems to have dropped out; [three] is supplied from what follows. The edition's reference II Tim. I appears to be an error for II Tim. II.

Scanning errors are read silently throughout, e.g. *creutor* as *creator*, *coenum* as *coenam*, *dejejunio* as *de jejunio*, *resur ectiones* as *resurrectiones*. Line 84: 'In Natali Domini et in Epiphania' is followed by separate instructions for Epiphany, so 'et in Epiphania' may be an intrusion. 'Facite illas sex missas et nocturnos' is awkward in the Epiphany provision and is rendered literally. *Schola* is left untranslated; it seems to mean the community's common room. *Resurrectio* here means a Gospel account of the resurrection. *Missae* in the final sentence of line 84 is taken as Masses, not sets of readings. Line 85: the distinction between *refectio* and *prandium* is unclear. *Bibituriae* and *caldelli* are rare words of uncertain sense; both seem to be drink measures. *Recentes* has no noun; it may mean fresh foods, possibly fresh fish. 'Olera formatico et oleo ... fercula condiantur' is syntactically difficult and the rendering is tentative. *Ista studeat obtemperare* is loose Latin; the sense is that the abbess should adapt these rules to the sisters' strength.

nodes.text: THE RULE OF ST AURELIAN FOR VIRGINS.
PROLOGUE.
To the holy sisters, venerable in Christ, established in the monastery of blessed Mary which, at God's command, we have built within the walls of the city of Arles, Bishop Aurelian [sends greeting].

By the inspiration of God, who goes before us with his ineffable mercy, you have resolved to repudiate the pleasures of the world, to despise and spurn temporal joys, and to choose the splendour of a most holy life; and, embracing the grace of virginity and chastity, and pursuing [it] out of love of God with all the eagerness of your inmost being and heart, to pierce your flesh with divine fear, holding to that saying: I have sworn and resolved to keep the judgments of your justice (Ps. 118); and, The world is crucified to me, and I to the world (Gal. 6). Therefore we have determined, at the Lord's command and as he works in us both to will and to accomplish, to build a monastery for you for the advancement of your souls, as we have also done. And so we have established a Rule for your discipline, which through you might teach [others] to run in the way of God's commandments, and might bring [you] happily to the kingdoms of heaven.
HERE BEGIN THE CHAPTERS OF THE RULE.

1. Whoever comes to conversion and asks to be received into the monastery, let the Rule first be read to her in the reception room; and when she has been received, let her not go out of the monastery until her death.
2. Let her not receive the religious habit unless she draws up deeds of her property to whomever she wishes.
3. Nothing is to be received secretly; but if anything has been sent and the one to whom it is sent does not need it, let it be put into the common stock and given to the one who needs it.
4. Letters are neither to be given nor received without the knowledge or permission of the abbess.
5. Let no one store near her bed anything that can be eaten or drunk.
6. Let no one have a private cell or cupboard.
7. There is to be no swearing.
8. There is to be no cursing.
9. There is to be no lying.
10. Anger is not to be held on to at all.
11. Let no sister lay a hand on a sister.
12. No one is permitted to go out to greet [visitors] except with the prioress or one of the seniors.
13. A slave woman is not to be admitted; a freedwoman, however, if she is one and the abbess so decides, may be admitted.
14. Neither men nor secular women are to enter the monastery, except into the basilica of the Lady Mary and into the reception room.
15. That not even the stewards themselves are permitted to enter the monastery, except for those needs which we have laid down in this Rule.
16. Infants are not to be received from baptism.
17. Those who are put in charge of an office are to receive the keys from upon the Gospels.
18. They are to succeed one another by turns in service, apart from the abbess and small children.
19. Let them not choose what work to do at their own pleasure, but [do] what has been ordered by the abbess or prioress.
20. While they work with their hands, let holy meditation not cease from the heart.
21. Let all things be common to you, and let no one presume to call or claim anything as her own.
22. Let them not wear clothes of any other colour than *laia* and *lactina*.
23. At vigils, care must be taken that no one falls asleep.
24. When the signal has been given, let no one come late.
25. While the psalms are being sung, let no one speak or work with her hands.
26. Let all learn their letters.
27. Let the holy abbess remain in the community.
28. If anyone is corrected or punished for any fault, let her not presume to answer back to the one rebuking her.
29. Have no quarrels.
30. The proud, the disobedient and those who prolong their anger are never to be spared.
31. The holy abbess is not permitted to sell or give away any of the property of the monastery, nor to do anything against the provisions of the Rule.
32. When seated at table, let them keep silent.
33. Let the holy abbess not take her meals outside the community.
34. Let them never take meat in their food.
35. Chickens and other fattened fowl are to be served only to the sick and the delicate; fish, however, on certain feast days.
36. Outside the common table no one is permitted to taste any food or drink, except the sick and children.
37. How the sick are to be attended to.
38. Where they are to say the day and night office.
39. That the holy abbess is to provide whatever is needed in sufficient measure.
40. That the holy community is to strive to fulfil all that has been laid down for it.
THE RULE.

CHAPTER ONE. At God's command we have first of all laid down that this is to be held inviolably: if anyone comes to conversion, let the Rule be read to her in the reception room, and if she professes that she will fulfil all of it, then let her be admitted. But once admitted, let her neither presume, nor be permitted, to go out of the monastery until her death, because of that prophetic saying: One thing I have asked of the Lord, this will I seek, that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life (Ps. 26).

II. Let her not receive the religious habit unless she draws up deeds of gift or sale to whomever she wishes, of all her property, whether great or small, because of the Lord's commands, where he says: If you wish to be perfect, sell all that you have (Matt. 19); and, If anyone does not leave all that he possesses, he cannot be my disciple (Luke 14).

III. Receive nothing secretly; but if any relative or friend gives or sends anything, in clothing or in gold or anything else whatever, let it be in the power of the holy abbess, and if the one to whom it is sent needs it, let it be given [to her]; but if she needs nothing, let it be put into the common stock and given to the one who needs it.
IV. We command that letters are neither to be given nor received without the knowledge or permission of the abbess.

V. Let no one presume to store near her bed anything that she can eat or drink, but let all put [such things] away in the common storeroom; and if ill health requires it, let what is needed not be refused her, at the order of a senior.
VI. No one is permitted to have a cell or cupboard, or anything of the kind that can be closed for her private use.

VII. Do not swear, because the Lord said: Do not swear (Matt. 5). And another scripture: A man who swears much will be filled with iniquity, and affliction will not depart from his house (Ecclus. 23).
VIII. Do not curse, because it is written: Nor will cursers possess the kingdom of God (1 Cor. 6).
IX. Lying is not permitted at all, because the mouth that lies kills the soul (Wisd. 1), and that saying: You will destroy those who speak falsehood (Ps. 5).

X. Let no one presume to prolong her anger until the next day. And, as human frailty will have it, if some rather harsh word has arisen between sisters, let them hasten to ask each other's pardon and forgive their debts, because of the Lord's command, where he says: If you remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift before the altar, and go first to be reconciled to your brother; and then you will come and offer your gift (Matt. 5). And, If you do not forgive men their sins, neither will your heavenly Father forgive you your sins (Matt. 6). Likewise, If he sins against you seven times in a day, and turns back and says, I repent, forgive him (Luke 17). And, I do not say to you up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven (Matt. 18). And another scripture: The anger of a man does not work the justice of God (Jas. 1). And the Apostle: Let the sun not go down on your anger (Eph. 4). If, which God forbid, at the devil's instigation anyone should be so filled with fury as to despise these commands with an obstinate heart, and one of those who are at odds should take the first step toward the other, asking her pardon, then if the one she asks does not forgive, let her receive discipline, so that she may correct herself toward charity. And if both have disdained [to do so], let both alike be suspended from communion or from food, until they are reconciled with each other.
XI. If a sister dares to lay a hand on a sister, let her receive discipline.

XII. No one is permitted to go out to greet [visitors] except with the abbess or prioress, or at least some other senior whom the abbess has instructed. And let them see or talk with their relatives in such a way that they do not speak in a raised voice.

XIII. A slave woman is not to be admitted; but if she is a freedwoman, still young in age, and comes with letters from her patron, let it be at the abbess's discretion whether she ought to be admitted.
XIV. Neither men nor secular women are to enter the monastery, except into the basilica of Blessed Mary and into the reception room.

XV. As for the stewards of the monastery, if they are in lay dress, not even they are to be permitted to enter, except for those needs which we have laid down in this Rule: let them enter with masons or carpenters, if anything needs to be made or repaired, or at least for some business of the abbess. Otherwise they are to have no permission or freedom to enter.
XVI. Let no one receive an infant from baptism.

XVII. Those to whom the keys of the storeroom, the wine cellar, the granary, the postern and the oratory are to be entrusted must be persons of proven character; and let them receive them from upon the altar or the Gospel, knowing that they will render an account to God for the service entrusted to them.

XVIII. In every service, or in the order of singing psalms, reading or working, let them succeed one another by turns, apart from the abbess. Except for the very old and small children, or at least those so ill that they cannot get up at all, [these] are not to be compelled to do what they are not able to do.
XIX. Let them not choose what work to do at their own pleasure, but let them do what the abbess has commanded.

XX. When you work with your hands throughout the whole day, let holy meditation not cease from the heart, on account of that [saying] of the Apostle: With psalms, hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your hearts to the Lord (Col. III).

XXI. Let no one presume to call anything her own, or to claim anything as her own property; but, according to the Acts of the Apostles, let all things be common to you; let there be one soul and one heart among you in the Lord (Acts IV).
XXII. Do not put on clothing of any other colour than *laia* [perhaps undyed wool] and milk-white.

XXIII. Let no one sleep at vigils. Indeed, if they are Sundays or feast days, let her to whom sleep comes stand while the others sit, so that she can drive off the drowsiness of sleep from herself, lest she be found either lukewarm or negligent in the work of God.

XXIV. When the signal has sounded, let all work be set aside, and, like the most prudent bees to the hive, strive to hurry with swift haste; if anyone comes too late, let her be subject to correction.

XXV. While the psalms are being sung, let your holy souls take care not to wander in mind, and moreover let them not presume to work or speak; but sing psalms wisely (Ps. XLVI), as the prophet said: I will sing psalms and I will understand (Ps. C), and that [saying]: I will sing psalms with the spirit, I will sing psalms with the mind also (I Cor. XIV), fearing that [saying]: Cursed is the man who does the work of God negligently (Jer. XLVIII).
XXVI. Let all learn letters.
XXVII. Let the holy abbess not stay away from the community.

XXVIII. If anyone is rebuked for any fault or transgression of the rule, or receives discipline, let her not presume to answer the one reproving her, because a sin that is corrected here is not punished at the eternal judgement. And you ought to accept the care of the soul in the way that a sick person accepts the care of a physician, holding to that [saying] of holy Scripture: He who casts off discipline is unhappy (Prov. XV). And that [saying]: I am ready for the scourges (Ps. XXXVII).
XXIX. Have no quarrels, holding to the precept of the Apostle, who says: The servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but be gentle (II Tim. I).
XXX. The proud and disobedient, and those who prolong their anger, are never to be spared until they are corrected.

XXXI. Let the holy abbess not be permitted to give away or sell anything of the monastery's property, nor to do anything against the provisions of the Rule. But if she attempts to do so, by holy counsel and with the one consent of the sisters, by our permission, do not give way to her; and do not allow this to be done on any account, because she should know that she will have to plead her case before God.

XXXII. Sitting at table, let them be silent, and let a reading be read every day at all times while food is taken. Let both the outer and the inner person be refreshed, the one by food and the other by the word of God, for it is written: Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God (Matt. IV).
XXXIII. Let the holy abbess not take her meals away from the community, unless illness is the cause.
XXXIV. Let meat never be taken as food.

XXXV. Let chickens or any fattened fowl not be served in the community, but let them be provided only for the sick and the delicate. Fish, however, may be procured on certain feasts, or when the abbess wishes to grant an indulgence.
XXXVI. Outside the common table let no one be permitted to taste any food or drink, apart from the sick and those who are younger in age.

XXXVII. The sick, however, are to be accommodated in such a way that, if it seems right to the holy abbess, they may even have a small storeroom of their own held in common, and a separate kitchen; and let care and attention be devoted to them until they recover.

XXXVIII. Let the community say the day and night office, that is, matins, vigils, nocturns, vespers and the twelfth [hour], in the basilica of the Lady Mary. But if the winter is harsh, say only matins, vespers and the twelfth [hour] in the aforesaid basilica, but the second, third, sixth and ninth [hours] in the inner oratory, for the sake of those who either wish to pray, or come to meet the abbess, or seek out their kinswomen. When any sister has died, let a few sisters keep watch over her in the oratory until midnight, and let *missae* [sets of readings with prayer] from the Apostle be held; after midnight, let those who have kept watch rest, and let others keep watch in turn; and bring this to the notice of the holy bishop, so that he may order her to be carried to the place where she is to be laid.

XXXIX. And since, by God's favour, a worthy and sufficient property has been conferred on you, one which can suffice for your monastery, before God and his angels I admonish and solemnly charge you, holy abbess, and you, venerable prioress, whoever you may be, that to the holy community which, by God's inspiration and command, lives by rule according to the provisions we have made, you supply with sufficiency all that is necessary for them in clothing and in food. If you neglect this, and they begin, under the compulsion of need, to murmur at all or to be in want, you should know that you will have to plead your case with me before the tribunal of Christ.

XL. And you, holy community, I adjure by your own progress and by almighty God to keep whole and unimpaired all that we have established in this Rule for the remedy of our soul and for the salvation of your souls. And so that you do not neglect anything through forgetfulness, read these things through once a month, that is, on the calends, and so twelve times in the year.
We have also judged that the order in which you ought to sing the psalms should be inserted in this little book.

On the first day of Easter at the third [hour], Kyrie eleison, twelve psalms: that is, let four sisters say two psalms each and a third, alleluiatic one; when the psalms have been said, Kyrie eleison, six antiphons, three readings: one from the Acts of the Apostles, another from the Apocalypse, the third from the Gospel; the hymn *Jam surgit hora tertia*, and the *capitellum* [short closing verse], then Kyrie eleison. In this way, in every work of God, say Kyrie eleison three times before you begin, and when the psalms have been said and when the *capitellum* has been said. At the sixth [hour] the same number of psalms, and one antiphon, the hymn *Jam sexta sensim volvitur*. A reading of the Gospel and the *capitellum*. At the ninth [hour] let the same order be kept, the hymn *Ter hora trina volvitur*. At the *lucernarium* [the lamp-lighting office] a short *directaneus* [a psalm said straight through], that is: Kingdoms of the earth, sing to God, sing psalms to the Lord (Ps. LXVII). On another day: Praise the Lord, you children; three antiphons; the hymn *Hic est dies verus Dei*, and the *capitellum*; say this hymn throughout Easter at matins and at the *lucernarium*. At the twelfth [hour], first a short *directaneus*: The sun has known its setting (Ps. CIII). Let six sisters say two psalms each with their alleluiatics; three antiphons, two readings, one from the Apostle, another from the Gospel. At the Easter nocturns say everything in the same number, as we have laid down for the twelfth [hour]. At matins, first the *directaneus*: I will exalt you, my God and my King. Then: Judge me, O God. O God, my God, I keep watch for you from the dawn, with alleluia; then: Give praise to the Lord, with alleluia; then: Let us sing to the Lord, with alleluia; afterwards: Praise the Lord, my soul. Praise the Lord, for a psalm is good. Praise the Lord, Jerusalem: all three with alleluia; then the *benedictio* [blessing] is to be said. After the *benedictio*: Praise the Lord from the heavens. Sing to the Lord a new song. Praise the Lord in his saints: with alleluia. My soul magnifies the Lord: either with an antiphon or with alleluia; the hymn *Gloria in excelsis Deo*; and the *capitellum*. And you will complete matins in this same order throughout Easter. So too on every Sunday, and on all the greater feasts on which you will be free from work. On ordinary days, however, at nocturns let the *directaneus* be said first: Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy; then eighteen psalms; three short antiphons, two readings from the Apostle or the Prophets, and the *capitellum*. When nocturns are completed you will say matins. In summer, that is, after Easter until the calends of October, the order will be the same. On Friday, however, after nocturns let two *missae* be held in summer; in winter three. For on Sunday, at all times, in summer and in winter, let six *missae* be held after nocturns. But if it happens that they rise rather late for vigils, let as much be read as seems good to the abbess. When the abbess gives the signal, let the one reading rise without delay, so that the canonical number of *missae* can be fulfilled. From the calends of October, however, further nocturns are to be added; at the first is to be said: Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy; at the second: Have mercy on me, O God, have mercy on me; eighteen psalms, two readings from the Prophets or from Solomon. The hymn at the first nocturns: *Rex aeterne Domine*; at the second: *Magna et mirabilia*. Then, after the second nocturns have been celebrated, because the nights are growing longer, hold three *missae* at the book every day. Let one sister read [three] pages or four, according to the measure of the book: if it is finely written, or of larger format, three pages; if of smaller, four, and let there be a prayer. Let her read the same amount again, and let there be another prayer; let her read the same amount a third time; and rise, say an antiphon from the psalms in order, then a responsory, then an antiphon. Let another sister read again; and when the three *missae* have thus been completed, say canonical matins: that is, first the canticle with an antiphon; then the *directaneus*: Judge me, O God. O God, my God, I keep watch for you from the dawn. Praise the Lord, my soul. Praise the Lord, for a psalm is good. Praise the Lord, Jerusalem; then: Praise the Lord from the heavens. Sing to the Lord a new song. Praise the Lord in his saints, with an antiphon. Say the hymn *Splendor paternae gloriae*; on another day *Aeterne lucis conditor*, and the *capitellum*, and Kyrie eleison twelve times. Let it be completed in this way on all ordinary days. After matins, at the first [hour] let six psalms be said, and the hymn *Fulgentis auctor aetheris*; two readings, that is, one from the Old and the other from the New Testament, and the *capitellum*. After this let all be free for reading until the third hour; for the remaining space of the day let them do their work, according to what the Lord said: My Father works until now, and I work (John V). And that [saying] of the Apostle: Working with our hands (I Thess. IV). And: Whoever does not work, let him not eat (II Thess. III). For it is written: The ways of the idle are strewn with thorns (Prov. XIII). And: Cast the useless servant into the outer darkness (Matt. XXV).

Again on ordinary days, at the third [hour], say six psalms, an antiphon, the hymn *Jam surgit hora tertia*, a reading and the *capitellum* *Fiat, Domine*. At the sixth [hour] the same number of psalms is to be kept; an antiphon is to be said, the hymn *Jam sexta sensim volvitur*, a reading and the *capitellum*. At the ninth [hour] this order is to be observed, but with the hymn *Ter hora trina volvitur*. At the *lucernarium* [the lamp-lighting office], at all times, on both feast days and ordinary days, first a *directaneus* [a psalm said straight through]; afterwards two antiphons. Let the third always be said with alleluia; the hymn on one day *Deus qui certis legibus*, on another day *Deus creator omnium*, and the *capitellum*. At the twelfth [hour] say eighteen psalms, an antiphon, a hymn, a reading and the *capitellum*. When you are about to go to rest, let compline be said in the *schola* in which you stay: first a *directaneus*, and let the ninetieth psalm be said, then the customary *capitella*. On the Nativity of the Lord and on Epiphany, rise at the third hour of the night: say one nocturn, and do six *missae* from the prophet Isaiah; again say a second nocturn, and let another six be read from the Gospel. On Epiphany as follows: first one nocturn; then do those six *missae* from the prophet Daniel and nocturns, and again six from the Gospel. Matins in the same order as we have written for Easter or for Sundays. On the feasts of martyrs let three or four *missae* be done: read the first *missa* from the Gospel, the rest from the passions of the martyrs. Every Friday after the twelfth [hour] let six *missae* be read from the book, and after nocturns three. Every Saturday at matins, *Cantemus Domino* and *Te Deum laudamus*. At the third [hour] let three readings be said: one from the Prophets, another from the Apostle, the third from the Gospel. Every Sunday after nocturns, when the first *missa* is read, that is, the resurrection, let no one presume to sit, but let all stand; on one Sunday one resurrection, on another Sunday another: in this way let all four resurrections be read in order on successive Sundays. After the third [hour], say the Our Father, and let all receive communion while singing psalms. Do the same on feast days as well. Masses shall be held whenever it seems good to the holy abbess.

We have also inserted the order of meals in this Rule. Daily, three dishes at the *refectio* [meal], two at the midday meal, at supper two *bibituriae* [drinks?]. At the *refectio* in summer, in the months of July and August, three *caldelli* [small measures of warm drink?], at the midday meal three, at supper at all times two each. But on feasts, and when the abbess wishes to grant indulgences, let her both order as much food as she wishes and add fresh [foods]. On ordinary days let the vegetables, with cheese and oil, always be seasoned as dishes. The fast from the calends of September to the calends of November is on Monday, Wednesday and Friday. From the calends of November to the Nativity of the Lord one is to fast daily, except on Saturday and Sunday. From Epiphany to Easter one is to fast daily, except on a major feast, Saturday and Sunday. After Easter until Pentecost one is to fast on Friday only. After Pentecost, in the months of June, July and August, let fast or midday meal be in the power of the abbess: as she sees what the sisters are able to bear, let her take care to comply in these matters.
